endorsements.quote: When addressing the risks of AI in the medical school curriculum, automation bias needs to be a discussion topic.

Students should still validate the results (to the extent that they can) from ChatGPT, because it can provide inaccurate results and the problem of hallucinations persists, before they wholeheartedly study or apply the wrong information.

Therefore, future physicians, medical students, and residents should be trained on the use of AI in health care and other related topics, such as big data or machine learning, to understand the tools they will be working with.

unlisted_practices: Incorporate AI education into the medical school curriculum, including the ethical issues of AI and the problem of automation bias.
Limit medical students' use of ChatGPT to certain appropriate tasks, such as summarizing information and generating practice questions, and do not make it the default or sole learning resource.
Do not use ChatGPT for reflective writing assignments or scientific writing in medical education.
Have faculty model critical questioning of AI outputs and avoid conveying AI solutionism through the hidden curriculum.
Do not ban ChatGPT in medical education; encourage moderate, supplementary use.
Ensure students still gain clinical and interpersonal experience with real patients and professionals rather than relying on ChatGPT-generated scenarios.

screen.reason: This is an editorial discussing the risks of automation bias when using ChatGPT in medical education and arguing for curriculum constraints and AI education.
